passage: In the school corridor, some boys were copying Yusuf's stammer. One held up a phone to film. Everyone laughed, and someone nudged Bidisha. "Laugh na!" Bidisha didn't. She looked at Yusuf's red face and his hands gripping his bag. She walked to the staffroom and told her teacher what she'd seen. The teacher came out; the phone went away quickly. Later, Bidisha sat next to Yusuf at lunch. He didn't say much, but he didn't leave.

qa.q: What were the boys copying?
qa.a: They were copying Yusuf's stammer.

qa.q: What might Yusuf have felt, judging by his face and hands?
qa.a: He likely felt ashamed and upset, with a red face and hands gripping his bag.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do that helped Yusuf?
qa.a: She refused to laugh, told a teacher and sat with him at lunch.

qa.q: How might the other boys see Bidisha after this?
qa.a: Some may be annoyed at her, but others might realise the teasing was wrong.

grounding: It shows a child recognising bullying, refusing to cheer it on and seeking adult help.

"Mama, some boys take Vikram's tiffin every day."
Sharmila looked up. "Every day?"
"Yes. And they laugh. Once I laughed too."
"Why did you laugh?"
Yash looked at the floor for a long time. "Everyone was. I didn't want them to laugh at me next."
"How do you think Vikram feels?"
"Bad. He eats nothing."
"So what can you do?"
"I could tell Ma'am. And not laugh."
"That's brave. Want me to come with you?"

qa.a: She asked questions that made Yash think about Vikram's feelings and Yash's own choices.

grounding: It shows a child recognising bullying, regretting joining in and deciding to seek adult help.

passage: I'm Omkar. Last year, when I was twelve, our class group chat turned mean. Some people kept posting a photo of Madhuri with silly drawings on it. Lots of kids sent laughing faces. My thumb actually hovered over one because everyone was doing it. Then I thought about Madhuri sitting at home, seeing all of it. I didn't send anything. I took screenshots and showed them to our class teacher the next morning. The group was shut down. Madhuri never knew it was me, and that's fine. I just didn't want to be one of the laughing faces.

qa.q: What did people keep posting in the group chat?
qa.a: A photo of Madhuri with silly drawings on it.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's thumb hover over the laughing face?
qa.a: Omkar felt pressure to join in because everyone else was doing it.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that helped stop the bullying?
qa.a: Omkar didn't join in, took screenshots and showed them to the class teacher.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel on learning that a classmate reported the posts?
qa.a: Madhuri would probably feel less alone and grateful someone cared. 🤍

grounding: It shows a child recognising online bullying, not joining in and reporting it to an adult.

passage: Class teacher's note, class four. At lunch today three boys were holding up Bittu's tiffin and chanting 'smelly, smelly' while others clapped. Ayesha was sitting close by. I watched from the corridor window. She did not clap. She looked at Bittu, whose ears had gone red, then got up and walked straight to the staff room. 'Ma'am, they're making fun of his food and he's almost crying,' she said. I went in with her. The chanting stopped. Later I spoke to the three boys and called Bittu's parents to reassure them. Tomorrow's circle time will be about what bystanders can do. I thanked Ayesha privately; she said, 'I was scared they'd laugh at me next.' — Kavitha Ma'am

qa.q: How could Kavitha Ma'am use circle time to support the class?
qa.a: She could help children name bullying, practise simple ways to get an adult and talk about not clapping along.

qa.q: What was the lunch like for Bittu before Ayesha acted?
qa.a: He was humiliated, with red ears and near tears, while classmates clapped at his food.

grounding: Shows a child identifying bullying, refusing to cheer it on and seeking adult help.

At the government school in Satna, every day at lunch, three older boys took Abhinav's tiffin and ate his parathas. They laughed while he stood there.
Farida, eleven, saw it for the third day. The others watched and giggled. Farida didn't.
“That's bullying,” she whispered to her friend.
She walked straight to the headmaster's room. “Sir, three boys take Abhinav's food every day.”
The headmaster came to the ground that same lunch. He spoke to the boys and sent a note to their parents. He asked Abhinav to eat near the staffroom that week and thanked Farida quietly.
Abhinav sat next to Farida the next day.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel the next day, sitting next to Farida?
qa.a: He probably feels safer and grateful that someone stood up for him.

I'm Eshaan. At the Wednesday break, a group of boys circled a new kid near the water cooler, copying his accent and grabbing his cap.

Irawati, you're asking what to do about the girls who tease your friend. Let me tell you what happened when I was your age.
There was a boy in my class called Sunder. He stammered. Every day, three boys made fun of him. The others laughed. I laughed too, at first.
One day I saw him crying behind the school wall. That night I couldn't sleep. The next morning, before class, I went to the headmaster and told him everything.
The headmaster called the three boys in that same morning and spoke to their parents. He moved Sunder to sit with me.
We stayed friends for forty years. That is your Yusuf nana's story.

qa.a: Sunder probably felt relieved and less alone, with a friend beside him.

The school bus was late in the pouring rain, and the older students were bored. Seema, eleven, saw two boys grab Jyoti's bag and toss it back and forth. Jyoti, eight, was crying.

Jyoti sat next to Seema on the bus.
